# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: inputs with NO scheme, and fully degenerate inputs.
This is the highest-risk area for divergence. Determine exactly what the parser does when there
is no '://'.
Probe at minimum: '' (empty string), ' ' (single space), 'a', 'a.com', 'a.com/', 'a.com/p',
'a.com:80', 'a.com:80/p', 'a.com?q=1', 'a.com#f', '/p', '/p?q', '//a.com', '//a.com/p',
'///a.com', '?q=1', '#f', ':80', ':', '::', ':::', '/', '//', '///', '////',
'localhost:8080', 'localhost:8080/p', 'user@host', 'user:pass@host',
'http:/a.com/p', 'http:a.com/p', 'http//a.com/p', 'httpx://a.com',
a 1-char string 'x', a string of only ':' repeated, a string of only '/' repeated,
a very long string (e.g. 100000 chars — build with perl and check for crash/timeout),
a string with embedded newline 'http://a\nb.com', embedded tab, embedded NUL is impossible in
argv so skip that, high-bit bytes 'http://\xff\xfe.com' (use perl exec), and a valid UTF-8
multibyte host 'http://ünïcödé.example/pä?q=ü'.
For every crash/abort record exit code and exact stderr. Also confirm: with NO argument at all
the program exits 1 and prints nothing; with EXTRA arguments only argv[1] is used.

content.text: Probing complete — 160+ inputs, zero crashes. Reporting findings.

input.dimension: Inputs with NO scheme, and fully degenerate inputs

rules.rule: The literal 3-byte substring "://" is the ONE AND ONLY trigger for scheme/authority parsing. If it is absent from the (fragment- and query-stripped) input, then scheme="", host="", port=-1, and path = the ENTIRE remaining string verbatim (including any leading '/', '//', '///', ':' or trailing characters). Nothing is ever promoted to host.

Order of operations is: (1) discard everything from the FIRST '#' to end-of-string; (2) split the remainder at the FIRST '?' -> query = everything after it, rest = everything before it; (3) search `rest` for the first "://". Consequently a "://" that lies after the first '?' or after the first '#' is NEVER treated as a scheme separator.
Fragment stripping happens BEFORE query splitting, so a '?' that appears after the first '#' produces NO query. This is the discriminating observation between "strip # first" and "split ? first".
The fragment is discarded entirely and is never exposed in any of the 5 fields. A trailing bare '#' or '?' is also just removed.
Query splitting uses only the FIRST '?'; subsequent '?' characters remain inside the query string.

An EMPTY scheme is legal and observable: if the input begins with "://", scheme="" but authority parsing DOES run, so host and port get populated. Therefore "no scheme" (no '://' anywhere) and "empty scheme" (leading '://') are different code paths that both print an empty line 1.
The scheme is taken as everything before the FIRST "://" occurrence, with no validation whatsoever — it may contain '/', ':', spaces, '@', digits, punctuation, or high-bit bytes.
Only the FIRST "://" is consumed; later "://" sequences are left in the authority/path.
The scheme (and only the scheme) is ASCII-lowercased. Host, path and query preserve case exactly. Bytes >= 0x80 are unaffected.
For the no-scheme case the port line is ALWAYS exactly the two bytes '-1'. A 'host:port'-looking string is never split; the colon stays in the path.

The fully-empty result ('', '', -1, '', '') is produced by many distinct inputs, so those inputs are mutually indistinguishable from the 5-line output: '' , '#', '?', '#f', '?#', '#?', '://', '://#f', '://:', '#a?b://c'.
rules.evidence:
'' -> od shows exactly the 7 bytes: 
 
 - 1 
 
 
. Identical byte-for-byte output from '#', '?', '#f', '://', '://#f', '://:'

rules.rule: There is NO whitespace trimming, NO percent-decoding, and NO path normalization anywhere. Whitespace and control bytes are preserved verbatim in the path.

Once a scheme is found, the authority is the substring up to the FIRST '/'; path is that '/' and everything after (empty if no '/' exists). Host is the part of the authority before its first ':'. A non-numeric or empty port yields -1.
Non-ASCII input is byte-transparent: raw high-bit bytes and multibyte UTF-8 pass through host/path/query unchanged, with no validation, punycoding or replacement.
Embedded newlines are not special to the parser — they are copied into the field, which makes the program emit MORE than 5 physical lines. This is a real gotcha for line-based harnesses.
rules.evidence:
'a
b.com' -> 6 physical lines: '', '', '-1', 'a', 'b.com', '' (path field contains the newline). 'http://a
b.com' -> 6 lines: 'http','a','b.com','-1','',''  (host field contains the newline). '
' alone -> 6 lines. Tab is likewise verbatim: 'a	b.com/p	q' -> ('','',-1,'a	b.com/p	q','')

rules.rule: No crashes, aborts, hangs or stderr output for ANY degenerate input tried. Exit code is always 0 when argv[1] exists, stderr is always 0 bytes, and behaviour is deterministic across repeated runs.
Long inputs are handled without truncation up to the OS limit. The only failure above ~131071 bytes is the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN (execve E2BIG), NOT a program limit.
rules.evidence: len 131071 -> exit=0, 131078 bytes of output (path length 131071 intact). len 131072 -> perl exec fails with 'Argument list too long' before the binary ever starts. len 100000 -> 100007 bytes output.

rules.rule: With NO argument at all the program prints nothing (0 bytes on stdout and stderr) and exits 1. With EXTRA arguments, only argv[1] is used; argv[2..] are ignored completely.
Common non-hierarchical / single-colon URI forms are NOT recognised as schemes (they lack '://') and land wholly in path.
'file:///etc/passwd' parses with an EMPTY host and the full absolute path (a very common divergence point).

Bracketed IPv6 literals are NOT special-cased: the host stops at the first ':' inside the brackets, yielding host '[' and port -1. In the no-scheme case the whole bracketed form just becomes the path.

uncertainties: Whether the implementation literally does find("://") on the query-stripped string, versus does find("://") on the original string and then rejects the hit if its index is after the first '?' or '#'. All probes I designed ('a?b://c', 'x?y://z#w', '#a?b://c', 'a?b#c://d', '?/a://b') give identical output under both models, so they are observationally equivalent. Either implementation reproduces every byte I observed.

Whether the fragment is truly discarded up-front versus stored in an inaccessible member. Not observable through these 5 accessors — 'a.com#f?q=1' -> query '' proves the '#' cut precedes the '?' split, which is all that matters behaviorally.

Whether scheme lowercasing uses std::tolower with the C locale or a hand-rolled ASCII fold. '\xC0\xDB://a' came back unchanged, which is consistent with the C locale (the default, since the driver never calls setlocale). Under an exotic LC_CTYPE the behavior could in principle differ; I did not vary LC_ALL.

Behavior for arguments longer than 131071 bytes is untestable via execve on Linux (MAX_ARG_STRLEN). If the reference implementation is exercised through a non-argv path (e.g. a library-level test), its behavior on multi-megabyte inputs is unverified here — though the 131071-byte run showed no sign of any internal length ceiling.

'://' with an empty scheme is indistinguishable from a missing scheme whenever the authority and path are also empty (e.g. '://' vs '' vs '#' vs '?' all print the identical 7 bytes). A reimplementation could take either code path for those inputs and still match.

I did not probe whether an empty-scheme authority applies default-port inference for a known scheme name (that is the port dimension's territory); I only confirmed no default port appears for 'http://a.com' (-1) or '://a.com' (-1).
